name: Medial elbow tendinopathy (golfer's elbow)
summary: A load-related overuse tendinopathy of the common flexor–pronator origin at the medial epicondyle, causing pain with wrist flexion, forearm pronation and gripping. Managed with education, load change and exercise.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Responds well to non-operative care in most people. In 20 refractory patients given eccentric exercise plus other measures, treatment lasted about 6 weeks on average (uncontrolled)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based, not time-based: pain-free gripping, pronation and full swing or throwing load; in a surgical series 9 of 30 elbows needed more than 6 months to reach maximum improvement

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Tenderness at the medial epicondyle plus pain on resisted forearm pronation (positive in 28 of 30 elbows in a surgical series) or resisted wrist flexion (12 of 30)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed to make the diagnosis. Use it to exclude other causes, such as a UCL injury, an avulsion or a bony problem

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: 40–60 years; usually less common than lateral elbow tendinopathy

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Prevalence of definite medial epicondylitis 0.4% in Finnish adults aged 30–64, compared with 1.3% for lateral epicondylitis

overview:
Medial elbow tendinopathy, commonly called golfer's elbow or medial epicondylitis, is a load-related overuse condition of the common flexor–pronator tendon at the medial epicondyle. It is the same story as lateral elbow tendinopathy on the other side of the joint: repeated forceful wrist flexion and forearm pronation load the origin faster than the tendon can adapt [r1,r2]. The name 'golfer's elbow' is a misnomer. Golf is only one context: throwing and manual work load the same origin, and in the general population the condition is linked to repetitive movement, forceful activity, smoking and obesity [r3,r1].

The pathology is degenerative rather than primarily inflammatory: a staged process of tendon change can progress to structural breakdown and fibrosis or calcification [r1,r2]. Diagnosis is clinical, with tenderness at the medial epicondyle and pain on resisted pronation or wrist flexion [r4]. Unlike its lateral counterpart, the ulnar nerve runs directly behind the medial epicondyle, so a coexisting ulnar neuropathy is common enough in surgical series to alter outcomes [r4].

First-line care is education, activity modification and progressive loading of the flexor–pronator mass [r1]. Direct trial evidence is thin. Corticosteroid injection gave short-term pain relief but no difference by 3 months or 1 year in a randomised trial [r5], and in lateral elbow tendinopathy the injection was linked to worse long-term outcomes [r6]. Most people settle with non-operative care; surgery is kept for persistent symptoms after 6 to 12 months [r2].

epidemiology.text: In a Finnish population sample of adults aged 30–64, the prevalence of definite medial epicondylitis was 0.4%, compared with 1.3% for lateral epicondylitis [r3]. A review gives prevalence of nearly 0.3–0.6% in men and 0.3–1.1% in women, and reports that epicondylitis is most common at 40–60 years and seems to affect women more than men; one population study found no sex difference, so the evidence on sex is mixed [r7,r3]. The consultation rate in general practice was about 0.1 per 100 people per year for medial epicondylitis [r7]. In golfers, lateral rather than medial elbow pain on the lead arm is the leading upper-extremity injury in amateurs, so do not assume that golfers have a medial problem [r8].

intrinsic: Smoking and obesity were each independently associated with medial epicondylitis in a Finnish population study [r3]
Condition on the dominant elbow was linked to a poorer prognosis (modifiers rather than causes) [r7]
extrinsic: Repetitive movements of the arms and forceful activities, each independently associated with medial epicondylitis [r3]
Occupational forceful activity, high force combined with high repetition, and awkward postures [r7]
Golf and throwing: athletes are most symptomatic in the late cocking and early acceleration phases of the throw [r1]
Poor swing or throwing mechanics and sudden rises in practice or throwing volume (clinical observation; consistent with the load-capacity model) [r9]

mechanism.summary: Medial elbow tendinopathy has no single injury moment. Flexor–pronator degeneration develops with repetitive forced wrist extension and forearm supination during activities that demand wrist flexion and forearm pronation, so the muscle group works eccentrically as the wrist is forced the other way and then concentrically to flex and pronate [r1]. In golf the trail arm flexes and pronates through impact; in throwing the load peaks in late cocking and early acceleration [r1]. When load repeatedly exceeds capacity the tendon moves from a reactive state towards disrepair and degeneration [r9].
sequence: The hand grips a club, ball or tool and the forearm flexor–pronator group contracts to hold the wrist and forearm in position.
At impact or release the wrist is forced towards extension and the forearm towards supination while the muscles are working, so they load eccentrically [r1].
Tension passes into the common flexor tendon and concentrates at its origin on the medial epicondyle [r1].
Repeated swings, throws or manual tasks without enough recovery, or a sudden rise in volume, push load above tendon capacity [r9].
Tenocytes respond, the matrix swells and collagen becomes disorganised, so the tendon thickens [r9].
With ongoing overload, a staged process of change can lead to structural breakdown and, in some cases, fibrosis or calcification [r1].
The tendon becomes sensitised: pain occurs at lighter loads, such as lifting a bag or shaking hands, and grip and pronation strength fall.

variants.name: Golf swing
variants.description: Repeated swings and heavy ground contact load the trail-arm flexor–pronator group at impact. Higher-handicap players tend to be injured through swing mechanics, whereas lower-handicap and professional players are injured by overuse [r8].

variants.name: Throwing and racquet serve
variants.description: Athletes are most symptomatic in late cocking and early acceleration [r1]. This is also when valgus load at the medial elbow is highest and the flexor–pronator mass acts as a dynamic stabiliser (anatomy), so always screen the ulnar collateral ligament in throwers.

variants.name: Occupational and manual loading
variants.description: Forceful activity, high force combined with repetition and awkward postures are the main occupational exposures [r7,r3].

variants.name: Load spike
variants.description: A sudden rise in practice, throwing or work volume, for example a new job or a pre-season block, can overload a tendon that lacks capacity [r9].

anatomy.text: The common flexor–pronator tendon arises from the anterior aspect of the medial epicondyle. It is formed by pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, flexor digitorum superficialis and flexor carpi ulnaris, with pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis usually the most affected. The ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) lies deep to the flexor–pronator mass and is the main static restraint to valgus load, while the mass acts as a dynamic stabiliser (standard anatomy). The ulnar nerve passes in the groove behind the medial epicondyle and through the cubital tunnel, so it lies close to the common flexor origin; coexisting ulnar neuropathy was present in 16 of 30 surgically treated elbows [r4]. The median nerve and the brachialis and biceps tendon lie anteriorly.

structures.name: Common flexor–pronator tendon
structures.role: Transmits tension from the wrist flexors and pronator teres to the medial epicondyle; the usual site of tendinopathy [r1]

structures.name: Pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis
structures.role: Forearm pronation and wrist flexion; the most frequently loaded components in golf and throwing

structures.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum superficialis
structures.role: Ulnar wrist flexion and finger flexion; contribute to the common origin and to grip

structures.name: Ulnar collateral ligament (anterior bundle)
structures.role: Primary static restraint to valgus stress; lies deep to the flexor–pronator origin and must be excluded in throwers (clinical reasoning)

structures.name: Ulnar nerve and cubital tunnel
structures.role: Runs directly behind the medial epicondyle; compression can coexist and worsens surgical results when moderate or severe [r4]

structures.name: Medial epicondyle (and apophysis in adolescents)
structures.role: Bony origin; in skeletally immature athletes the apophysis is the weak link, giving Little League elbow rather than a tendinopathy

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Medial elbow tendinopathy is a failure of the common flexor–pronator tendon to adapt to load, not a rupture. Flexor–pronator degeneration is related to repetitive overuse and underlying tendinopathy, and a staged process of pathological change can end in structural breakdown, irreparable fibrosis or calcification [r1,r2]. In the continuum model, repeated overload of a tendon with insufficient capacity produces a reactive response, then disrepair with matrix disorganisation, and in some people a degenerative state [r9]. The model has since been revisited, because structure and pain do not map neatly onto each other, so pain, function and structure should be weighed together [r10].

Intra-operative descriptions in a surgical series noted an inflammatory focus in 17 of 30 elbows and focal ulnar-nerve compression in 9 [r4], which shows that the picture is not purely degenerative in every refractory case. The accepted working model is nevertheless a degenerate, thickened tendon rather than a primary tendonitis [r2]. Direct histological and imaging evidence for medial disease is sparser than for the lateral elbow, so many statements here are extrapolated from the wider tendinopathy literature.

structures.name: Common flexor–pronator tendon
structures.effect: Thickened, disorganised tendon at the medial epicondyle, with possible fibrosis or calcification in long-standing cases [r1]

structures.name: Tendon-bone enthesis (medial epicondyle)
structures.effect: Site of focal tenderness; all 30 operated elbows had tenderness over the medial epicondyle [r4]

structures.name: Ulnar nerve
structures.effect: Coexisting ulnar neuropathy was present in 16 of 30 operated elbows. Moderate or severe neuropathy was associated with poorer surgical results [r4].

structures.name: Ulnar collateral ligament
structures.effect: May be stressed in throwers and must be separated from tendinopathy by valgus stress testing and, if needed, imaging [r1]

muscles.name: Pronator teres and wrist flexors
muscles.effect: Pain-related weakness of pronation and grip. Resisted pronation was the most sensitive provocative test, positive in 28 of 30 elbows, and resisted wrist flexion was positive in 12 of 30 [r4].

muscles.name: Forearm extensors
muscles.effect: Act as antagonists and take part in the eccentric phase; balanced strengthening is part of the programme (clinical reasoning)

muscles.name: Scapular and trunk muscles
muscles.effect: In throwing and golf the proximal chain and trunk rotation set how much load reaches the elbow; deficits shift load to the forearm (clinical reasoning; not tested in the sources reviewed)

cellular.timing: Days to weeks after a load spike
cellular.description: Tenocytes activate and produce proteoglycan, so the matrix takes up water and the tendon thickens. This short-term adaptive change can reverse if load is adjusted [r9].
Cell numbers and protein production rise as the tendon attempts repair; collagen becomes more disorganised [r9].
Areas of cell death and disorganised matrix; structural breakdown and fibrosis or calcification may follow [r9,r1].

cellular.timing: Weeks to months of progressive loading
cellular.description: Tissue-level adaptation was not measured in the medial elbow sources reviewed. Improvement in pain and function after eccentric exercise has been reported (see management) [r11].

systems.effect: Pain at the medial epicondyle can sensitise over time, and the ulnar nerve may be involved in some people; screen for neuropathy [r4]. Central sensitisation was not examined in the medial sources reviewed.
Shoulder, trunk and wrist mechanics in the swing or throw set elbow load. Swing modification directed by a teaching professional is supported for upper-extremity golf injuries [r8].
Obesity and smoking were each independently associated with medial epicondylitis. Whether changing them alters the course is untested [r3].
Combined forceful, repetitive, awkward-posture work predicts onset, and high physical strain, non-neutral wrist posture and dominant-arm involvement predict a poorer prognosis [r7].

grading.system: Tendinopathy continuum (Cook and Purdam): a structural staging model, used alongside pain and function [r10]

grades.description: Short-term adaptive response to a load spike: thickened but otherwise intact tendon with pain that rises quickly with load [r9].
grades.prognosis: Often settles with load adjustment followed by gradual re-exposure

grades.description: Attempted repair with more matrix disorganisation if overload continues [r9].
grades.prognosis: Responds to progressive loading; some change can partly reverse

grades.description: Focal areas of cell death and disorganised matrix, with possible fibrosis or calcification [r9,r1].
grades.prognosis: Structure rarely normalises, but capacity can be rebuilt and pain reduced; recovery is slower

timeframes.summary: The continuum describes load history, not a calendar, so the stage durations are illustrative and overlap. Medial and lateral epicondylitis respond well to non-operative management, and surgery is considered if 6–12 months of non-operative care fails [r2].

healing.description: Tenocyte activation and matrix swelling after a load spike; settles with load adjustment [r9]
Attempted repair with matrix disorganisation if overload continues [r9]
Cell death and disorganised matrix, with possible fibrosis or calcification in long-standing overload [r1]
In 20 patients with refractory disease, an eccentric-based programme lasted 6.1 weeks on average (range 1–10) [r11]. Typical clinical range 6–12 weeks, longer when chronic.

milestones.label: 6-week review
milestones.note: Steroid injection gave significantly less pain at 6 weeks than saline, with both groups also receiving physical therapy and NSAIDs [r5]

milestones.label: Eccentric programme complete in refractory cases
milestones.note: Average treatment duration 6.1 weeks; DASH 34.7 to 7.9 (uncontrolled series of 20) [r11]

milestones.label: 3-month review
milestones.note: No difference in pain between steroid and saline injection groups by 3 months [r5]

milestones.label: 6–12-month decision point
milestones.note: Consider specialist review and surgical options if 6–12 months of non-operative care has failed [r2]

milestones.label: 1-year review
milestones.note: No difference between steroid and saline injection groups at 1 year, which the authors attribute to the natural history [r5]

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based; there is no standard time. Many people continue to work and play with load modification. If 6–12 months of well-delivered non-operative care fails, surgery is an option, and in a surgical series nine of 30 elbows needed more than 6 months to reach maximum improvement [r2,r4].

symptoms: Pain at the inner elbow (medial epicondyle), sometimes spreading into the flexor forearm
Pain triggered by gripping, lifting with the palm down or up, carrying bags, shaking hands, using tools and swinging a golf club or throwing [r1]
Gradual onset over weeks, often after a change in practice volume, equipment, technique or work
Reduced or painful grip, and morning stiffness
In some people tingling or numbness in the ring and little fingers, which suggests ulnar nerve involvement [r4]
signs: Focal tenderness at the medial epicondyle and just distal to it over the flexor–pronator origin [r4]
Pain on resisted forearm pronation and on resisted wrist flexion [r4]
Pain on passive wrist extension with the elbow extended and the forearm supinated (tendon stretch)
Reduced pain-free grip strength compared with the other side
Full elbow range, no effusion and no valgus laxity; check the ulnar nerve for Tinel's sign and sensory change

subjective: Pain site and behaviour: medial epicondyle and flexor mass versus inner elbow joint line (UCL) versus nerve symptoms [r1]
Aggravating tasks: golf swing, throwing phase (late cocking or early acceleration), lifting, tool use, carrying [r1]
Recent load change: practice volume, new club or tool, technique change or a return after a break
Duration, previous treatment and response, including any injection
Ulnar nerve symptoms: tingling in the ring and little fingers, night paraesthesia, clumsiness or weakness, because neuropathy affects management and surgical results [r4]
Neck and shoulder symptoms, smoking status, weight and occupation [r3]
Age and skeletal maturity: in adolescents suspect apophysitis or an avulsion instead (see Little League elbow)
observation: Forearm muscle bulk, elbow carrying angle and swelling over the medial epicondyle (swelling suggests another cause)
Task observation: golf swing, throwing mechanics, tool grip and workstation set-up
Posture and trunk or shoulder mechanics that increase elbow valgus load (clinical observation)
palpation: Tenderness at the medial epicondyle and just distal and anterior to it over the flexor–pronator origin; all 30 patients in a surgical series had medial epicondylar tenderness [r4]
UCL: tenderness just distal to the epicondyle over the sublime tubercle and along the ligament (see differentials)
Ulnar nerve in the groove and cubital tunnel: tenderness, Tinel's sign, thickening or subluxation on flexion
rangeOfMotion: Elbow flexion, extension, pronation and supination are usually full; loss of extension or a block suggests an intra-articular cause
Passive wrist extension with the elbow extended and forearm supinated stretches the flexor–pronator origin and often reproduces pain
Cervical and shoulder range, to screen the proximal chain and for referred pain
strength: Resisted forearm pronation: pain and force; the most sensitive provocative test in a surgical series, positive in 28 of 30 elbows [r4]
Resisted wrist flexion: positive in 12 of 30 elbows in the same series [r4]
Pain-free grip strength with a dynamometer, compared with the other side
Finger abduction and adduction, thumb–index pinch and first dorsal interosseous bulk if ulnar neuropathy is suspected [r4]
neuro: Ulnar nerve screen: sensation in the ring and little fingers, Tinel's sign at the cubital tunnel, elbow flexion test, intrinsic hand strength
Median nerve screen if pronator teres syndrome is suspected: pain and paraesthesia in the median distribution, provoked by resisted pronation
Cervical screen for C7–C8 radiculopathy: neck movements, Spurling-type provocation, reflexes and myotomes
functional: Pain with a standard grip task, such as lifting a weighted bag or jug
Task-specific provocation: golf swing, throwing, tool use or racquet serve

specialTests.name: Palpation of the medial epicondyle and common flexor origin
specialTests.purpose: Localise pain to the flexor–pronator origin
specialTests.procedure: With the elbow flexed to about 90° and the forearm supported, palpate the medial epicondyle and the tissue just distal and anterior to it. Compare with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Focal tenderness that reproduces the familiar pain. All 30 patients in a surgical series had tenderness at this site, so a negative palpation makes the diagnosis unlikely in that population [r4].
specialTests.sensitivity: 30 of 30 elbows in a surgical series (no control group)

specialTests.name: Resisted forearm pronation
specialTests.purpose: Load the pronator teres and flexor–pronator origin
specialTests.procedure: With the elbow flexed to 90° and the forearm in neutral, the patient pronates against the examiner's resistance while the examiner palpates the medial epicondyle.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of medial epicondylar pain. Positive in 28 of 30 surgically treated elbows (the most sensitive provocative test in that series). Specificity was not reported [r4].
specialTests.sensitivity: 28 of 30 elbows in a surgical series (no control group)

specialTests.name: Resisted wrist flexion
specialTests.purpose: Load the wrist flexors at their origin
specialTests.procedure: With the elbow extended or flexed and the forearm supinated, the patient flexes the wrist against resistance while the examiner palpates the medial epicondyle.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of medial epicondylar pain. Positive in 12 of 30 surgically treated elbows, so a negative test does not exclude the diagnosis [r4].
specialTests.sensitivity: 12 of 30 elbows in a surgical series (no control group)

specialTests.name: Passive wrist extension stretch (elbow extended, forearm supinated)
specialTests.procedure: With the elbow extended and the forearm supinated, the examiner extends the wrist while palpating the medial epicondyle.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of medial epicondylar pain. No accuracy data were identified in the sources reviewed.

specialTests.name: Valgus stress and moving valgus stress tests
specialTests.purpose: Exclude UCL injury as the main source in throwers
specialTests.procedure: With the elbow flexed to about 30° and the forearm supinated, apply a valgus force; for the moving test, flex and extend the elbow under a maintained valgus load.
specialTests.positive: Medial elbow pain or laxity at the UCL rather than at the epicondyle. Accuracy figures were not identified in the sources reviewed.

specialTests.name: Ulnar nerve screen (Tinel's sign and elbow flexion test)
specialTests.procedure: Tap over the ulnar nerve in the cubital tunnel, then hold the elbow fully flexed with the wrist extended for 30–60 s and ask about tingling in the ring and little fingers.
specialTests.positive: Paraesthesia in the ulnar distribution. Accuracy figures were not identified in the sources reviewed; coexisting ulnar neuropathy was present in 16 of 30 operated elbows [r4].

clinicalRules.name: Clinical diagnosis
clinicalRules.description: Diagnosis rests on pain at the medial epicondyle with tenderness at the flexor–pronator origin and pain on resisted pronation or wrist flexion, after excluding UCL injury, ulnar nerve compression and cervical referral [r1,r4]. No validated clinical prediction rule was identified in the sources reviewed.

outcomeMeasures.name: DASH or QuickDASH
outcomeMeasures.use: Upper-limb disability questionnaire used in the medial elbow case series: scores fell from 34.7 to 7.9 after eccentric exercise in 20 refractory patients [r11]

outcomeMeasures.name: Pain-free grip strength (dynamometer)
outcomeMeasures.use: Capacity measure to guide loading; compare with the other side (clinical convention)

outcomeMeasures.name: Pain intensity (NRS 0–10) with a standard grip or pronation task
outcomeMeasures.use: Simple provocation measure; the Nirschl pain-grading system has been used in trials [r5]

outcomeMeasures.name: Sport-specific measures
outcomeMeasures.use: DASH sports module used in the medial elbow case series [r11]; add a swing or throw count and next-day pain log

outcomeMeasures.name: Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation (PRTEE)
outcomeMeasures.use: Developed for lateral elbow tendinopathy; it is sometimes adapted for medial symptoms, but validity in medial disease was not examined in the sources reviewed

imaging.indication: After trauma, in adolescents, or if a bony cause is suspected (loose body, spur, calcification, avulsion)
imaging.findings: Usually normal; calcification in the flexor origin occurs in long-standing disease [r1]

imaging.indication: Diagnosis uncertain, or to guide a procedure
imaging.findings: Tendinosis was confirmed using echotexture, interstitial tears and neovascularity in a refractory case series [r12]

imaging.indication: Suspected UCL injury, partial tear or avulsion, nerve compression, or surgical planning
imaging.findings: Shows the flexor–pronator origin, the UCL and the cubital tunnel. A staged process of tendon change, with fibrosis or calcification late, is described [r1].

differentials.name: Ulnar collateral ligament injury (thrower's elbow)
differentials.distinguishing: Throwers with medial elbow pain at the UCL (just distal to the epicondyle) that is worst in late cocking and early acceleration, with valgus laxity or pain on the valgus stress tests. It can coexist with tendinopathy (clinical reasoning).

differentials.name: Cubital tunnel syndrome (ulnar neuropathy)
differentials.distinguishing: Ring and little finger paraesthesia, a positive Tinel's sign or elbow flexion test, and intrinsic weakness in advanced cases. It coexisted with medial epicondylitis in 16 of 30 surgical elbows and worsened results when moderate or severe [r4].

differentials.name: Little League elbow (medial epicondyle apophysitis)
differentials.distinguishing: Skeletally immature thrower with pain at the medial epicondyle apophysis; radiographs may show widening or fragmentation. Consider this in athletes under about 16 years.

differentials.name: Lateral elbow tendinopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Pain over the lateral epicondyle with resisted wrist extension. The two can coexist and share risk factors [r3].

differentials.name: Cervical radiculopathy (C7–C8)
differentials.distinguishing: Neck pain, symptoms reproduced by neck movement and dermatomal, myotomal or reflex change.

differentials.name: Pronator teres syndrome (median nerve compression)
differentials.distinguishing: Aching in the proximal anterior forearm with median-distribution paraesthesia, provoked by resisted pronation with the elbow flexed.

differentials.name: Medial epicondyle avulsion or fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Acute valgus injury or a sudden pop, with swelling, bruising and bony tenderness; imaging shows the fragment.

differentials.name: Posteromedial olecranon impingement or elbow osteoarthritis
differentials.distinguishing: Posteromedial pain with elbow extension, especially in throwers, with a loss of extension and bony changes on imaging.

redFlags: Acute medial elbow pain with a pop or valgus force, swelling, bruising, or inability to continue throwing: suspect UCL rupture, a medial epicondyle avulsion or a fracture. Arrange radiographs and urgent orthopaedic review.

Progressive ulnar nerve signs: persistent numbness in the ring and little fingers, weakness of finger abduction or pinch, or wasting of the first dorsal interosseous: refer for urgent nerve conduction studies and surgical review, because moderate or severe neuropathy worsened results [r4].
Neck-arm pain with arm weakness, spreading numbness, reflex change or signs of myelopathy (clumsy hands, gait change): refer for urgent spinal assessment.
A hot, red, swollen elbow with fever or systemic illness: suspect septic arthritis or infection. Refer for same-day emergency assessment.
Constant night or rest pain unrelated to load, unexplained weight loss, or a history of cancer: suspect a bone or soft-tissue tumour or inflammatory disease. Arrange imaging and medical review.
No improvement after 6–12 months of well-delivered non-operative care: discuss surgical options with a doctor [r2].

management.principles: Treat medial elbow tendinopathy as a load-capacity problem in a person. Explain the condition, modify the aggravating tasks and technique instead of stopping everything, and build capacity with progressive flexor–pronator loading once the acute symptoms ease [r1]. The sources reviewed identified only one placebo-controlled injection trial and uncontrolled case series for the medial elbow [r5,r11]; much of the loading advice is extrapolated from lateral elbow tendinopathy and other tendons, where exercise outperformed corticosteroid injection and passive treatment with low certainty [r13]. Check the ulnar nerve in every patient, because coexisting neuropathy changes the plan [r4]. In throwers and golfers, review mechanics and equipment with a coach [r8]. Medial and lateral epicondylitis usually respond well to non-operative care, and surgery is kept for people whose symptoms persist after 6–12 months [r2].

medical.name: Corticosteroid injection
medical.description: In a randomised, double-blind trial of 58 patients (60 elbows), 40 mg methylprednisolone with lidocaine produced significantly less pain than saline at 6 weeks, but no difference at 3 months or 1 year; the authors attributed the improvement in both groups to the natural history [r5]. Reviews report moderate short-term relief without long-term benefit [r2]. In lateral elbow tendinopathy, injection led to worse recovery and more recurrence at 26 and 52 weeks, and no equivalent medial trial exists [r6]. Injecting near the ulnar nerve also carries a nerve risk (clinical caution).

medical.name: NSAIDs and simple analgesia
medical.description: Oral or topical NSAIDs are part of non-surgical supportive care [r1]. They give moderate symptomatic relief in the short term but no demonstrated long-term benefit [r2]. Use briefly to allow loading.

medical.name: Autologous blood or platelet-rich plasma injection with dry needling
medical.description: An uncontrolled series of 20 patients with refractory medial epicondylitis reported lower pain and improved ultrasound appearance at 10 months after ultrasound-guided dry needling and autologous blood injection [r12]. In the lateral elbow, a Cochrane review found these injections give little or no clinically important benefit over placebo, and no medial randomised trial was identified [r14].

medical.name: Surgery (open debridement of the flexor–pronator origin, with ulnar nerve decompression or transposition when indicated)
medical.description: Reserved for persistent symptoms after 6–12 months of non-operative care [r2]. In a retrospective series of 30 elbows, 87% (26 elbows) had good or excellent results at an average of 7 years, but only 2 of 5 elbows with moderate or severe associated ulnar neuropathy did well compared with 24 of 25 with none or mild neuropathy [r4]. Surgical efficacy has not been tested in randomised trials [r7].

physio.name: Education and load or technique modification (not rest)
physio.description: Explain the condition and agree on goals, reduce or redistribute the loads and swings or throws that provoke pain, and adjust technique, grip and equipment. Workload modification should be considered, especially in manually strenuous jobs [r7,r1]. Swing modification directed by a teaching professional is supported for upper-extremity golf injuries [r8].

physio.name: Progressive flexor–pronator loading (isometric, then isotonic, then heavy slow and functional)
physio.description: After the acute symptoms ease, rehabilitation of the flexor–pronator mass and injury prevention are the focus of care [r1]. The evidence is largely extrapolated: in lateral elbow tendinopathy, exercise outperformed corticosteroid injection and passive treatments, with low or very low certainty and small effects [r13]. No randomised trial of loading in medial elbow tendinopathy was identified.

physio.name: Eccentric wrist flexor exercise (FlexBar)
physio.description: In an uncontrolled series of 20 patients who had failed earlier treatment, adding an eccentric wrist flexor exercise (3 × 15 twice daily) to stretching, ultrasound, cross-friction massage, heat and ice reduced DASH from 34.7 to 7.9 over an average of 6.1 weeks. Other treatments were given at the same time and there was no control group [r11].

physio.name: Bracing, counterforce straps and taping
physio.description: Sometimes used to offload the origin in the short term. Evidence for the medial elbow was not identified in the sources reviewed.

physio.name: Ulnar nerve management (education, positioning, night extension splint, nerve glides)
physio.description: Applies when ulnar neuropathy coexists. It was present in 16 of 30 surgical elbows and affected surgical outcome [r4]. Avoid prolonged elbow flexion and leaning on the medial elbow. Evidence for conservative nerve treatment was not examined in the sources reviewed.

physio.name: Passive treatment alone (rest, ice, therapeutic ultrasound, massage)
physio.description: In lateral elbow tendinopathy, exercise outperformed passive interventions [r13]. Passive treatment does not build capacity and should not replace loading (extrapolated; no medial trial).

education: This is an overloaded, thickened tendon at the inner elbow, not a torn tendon and not just inflammation. Its capacity can be rebuilt with progressive loading.
Most people improve with non-operative care, but it can take months. Keep to the programme even when you feel better.
A cortisone injection gave short-term relief only in the medial elbow trial, and in the lateral elbow people who had one did worse in the long term, so it is not advised as a first step.
Keep using the arm: lift with the palm up or both hands, use lighter loads and thicker handles, and review your golf or throwing technique with a coach instead of resting completely.
Some pain with exercise is acceptable if it settles within 24 hours. Pain that is clearly worse the next day means the load was too high.
Tell us about any tingling or numbness in the ring and little fingers, because the ulnar nerve runs behind the inner elbow and may need to be treated too.

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based and follows the load-capacity model: settle irritability and modify technique, build flexor–pronator and grip capacity, add heavy and functional loading, then rebuild golf, throwing or work exposure. Move on when the objective criteria are met, not when a number of weeks has passed. Dosages below are typical clinical ranges, extrapolated from tendinopathy loading practice and from the lateral elbow; only the eccentric FlexBar dose comes from a medial case series [r11]. As a working rule (clinical convention), pain during exercise should stay at or below about 4/10 and settle within 24 hours. Screen the ulnar nerve at every stage, and review adherence at every visit.

stages.name: Settle pain & modify load
goals: Reduce pain with gripping and swing or throw
Explain the condition and agree on goals
Modify the tasks, technique and equipment that aggravate
Keep the rest of the arm, shoulder and trunk conditioned
precautions: Avoid repeated painful forceful flexion and pronation; do not rest completely [r1]
Do not stretch hard into pain
Avoid corticosteroid injection as a first step [r5]
Keep pain at or below about 4/10 (clinical convention); stop and review if ulnar nerve symptoms appear

exercises.name: Isometric wrist flexion hold (forearm supported)
exercises.dosage: 5 × 30–45 s at about 50–70% effort, 1–2 times daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Push steadily and breathe normally. Pain should be steady or fall during the hold.

exercises.name: Isometric forearm pronation hold
exercises.dosage: 5 × 30–45 s at about 50–70% effort, 1–2 times daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Elbow at 90°, forearm neutral; resist with the other hand

exercises.name: Pain-free grip squeeze (putty or ball)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10 holds of 5 s at a pain-free grip, daily
exercises.cues: Squeeze to just before pain; keep the wrist neutral

exercises.name: Task and technique modification
exercises.cues: Lift with the palm up or both hands, use thicker handles and shorten practice blocks

exercises.name: Band row (scapular and shoulder capacity)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10–12, 3 s lowering, daily or every second day
exercises.cues: Squeeze the shoulder blades back and keep the wrist neutral

progressionCriteria: Pain on resisted wrist flexion and pronation at or below 3/10
Pain-free grip improving week on week
Daily tasks (lifting a bag, shaking hands) are mild or pain-free
Pain settles within 24 hours of exercise

stages.name: Build tendon capacity
goals: Increase wrist-flexor, pronator and grip strength
Raise tolerance to repeated gripping and swing loads
Restore normal use of the arm at work and home
precautions: Increase load only when the previous session settles within 24 hours
Keep the forearm supported and the movement slow and controlled
Avoid sustained full elbow flexion if ulnar symptoms are present

exercises.name: Wrist flexion with dumbbell (forearm supported)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 12–15, 3 s up and 3 s down, once daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Slow, controlled lowering; stop short of sharp pain

exercises.name: Eccentric wrist flexion with a flexible rubber bar (FlexBar)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 15, twice daily (the dose used in the medial elbow case series) [r11]
exercises.cues: Twist the bar with the uninvolved hand, then slowly release with the painful wrist flexors

exercises.name: Forearm pronation with a hammer or weighted bar
exercises.cues: Hold near the handle end first, then lengthen the lever

exercises.name: Progressive grip squeeze
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10 holds of 6–8 s, building resistance, daily
exercises.cues: Add resistance only when pain stays at or below 4/10

progressionCriteria: Pain on loaded wrist flexion and pronation at or below 3/10
Completes 3 × 15 slow repetitions with no next-day flare
Pain-free grip about 70–80% of the other side, or clearly improving (clinical convention)
DASH or QuickDASH falling from baseline

stages.name: Heavy slow & functional strength
goals: Build high-load strength in the flexor–pronator group and forearm
Restore tolerance to carrying, pulling and weight-bearing through the hand
Rebuild confidence in gripping, swinging and throwing
precautions: Progress load in small steps and keep a slow tempo
Avoid sudden jumps in carrying or throwing load

exercises.name: Heavy slow wrist flexion
exercises.dosage: 3–4 × 6–10, 3 s up and 3 s down, 2–3 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Load that makes the last 2 repetitions hard but controlled

exercises.name: Farmer carry
exercises.cues: Tall posture, neutral wrist, even grip

exercises.name: Push-up
exercises.cues: Keep the wrists neutral and elbows controlled

exercises.name: Heavy row
exercises.cues: Control the lowering; do not clench the grip

exercises.name: Grip endurance with a tool
exercises.dosage: 3 sets of 30–60 s of tool use or squeeze, 2–3 times a week

progressionCriteria: Pain at or below 2/10 on heavy wrist flexion, pronation and carrying
Pain-free grip about 80–90% of the other side (clinical convention)
Everyday tasks, lifting and carrying are pain-free or mild
No next-day flare after the heaviest session

stages.name: Return to golf, throwing and work
goals: Return to full swing, throwing or tool use
Rebuild exposure in graded steps with technique review
Hold strength and manage load for the long term
precautions: Increase swings, throws or work hours stepwise, tracking next-day pain
Do not return to full competition while pain is above 2/10 or flares the next day
Avoid sudden load spikes after a break or tournament

exercises.name: Graded golf programme (putting, chipping, half swings, full swings)
exercises.dosage: Start with 10–20 half-swings and build in steps of roughly 10–20% a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Avoid heavy ground contact early; review grip pressure and swing mechanics with the coach [r8]

exercises.name: Graded throwing programme (interval throwing)
exercises.dosage: Short-distance, low-intensity throws building distance and intensity over 4–8 weeks, if the sport requires it (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Stop if medial elbow pain or ulnar symptoms recur

exercises.name: Graded task-specific loading (tools, carrying, manual work)
exercises.dosage: Start at a fraction of usual work volume and build in steps of roughly 10–20% a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Pace tasks, take micro-breaks and keep the wrist neutral

exercises.name: Heavy strength maintenance (wrist flexion, row, carry)

progressionCriteria: Completes full practice, match or work for at least 2 weeks with pain at or below 2/10 and no next-day flare
Pain-free grip about 90% or more of the other side (clinical convention)
DASH or QuickDASH near the patient's goal, with no pain on resisted pronation or wrist flexion
Technique and equipment reviewed and patient confident

criteria: No validated, tendinopathy-specific return-to-activity criteria were identified in the sources reviewed; the criteria below reflect clinical convention and trial design
Pain on resisted wrist flexion, pronation and the usual provocation task at or below 2/10, with no next-day flare
Pain-free grip about 90% or more of the other side or of pre-injury values (clinical convention)
No ulnar nerve symptoms and no valgus laxity or UCL tenderness (throwers)
Tolerates at least 2 weeks of full-volume practice or work without a rise in pain
Technique and equipment reviewed, and a maintenance strength and load-management plan is in place [r8]
tests: Pain-free grip strength (dynamometer) compared with the other side
Resisted wrist flexion and pronation pain (0–10)
Task-specific trial: golf swings, throws or tool use at full intensity with a next-day pain log
Ulnar nerve screen (Tinel's sign, elbow flexion test)

prognosis: Medial elbow tendinopathy usually responds to non-operative care, and in a randomised injection trial both the steroid and saline groups improved, which the authors attributed to the natural history of the disorder [r5,r2]. People with high physical strain at work, non-neutral wrist postures or dominant-arm involvement have a poorer prognosis [r7]. Coexisting ulnar neuropathy is important for outcome: in a surgical series, 24 of 25 elbows with none or mild neuropathy had a good or excellent result, compared with 2 of 5 with moderate or severe neuropathy, and nine of 30 elbows needed more than 6 months for maximum improvement [r4]. Long-term recurrence rates for the medial elbow were not identified in the sources reviewed.
prevention: Build practice, throwing and work volume gradually after a break or when starting a new job, tool or sport, because sudden rises in load overload the tendon [r9].

Review swing or throwing mechanics and equipment with a coach. Higher-handicap golfers tend to be injured through swing mechanics, and swing modification is supported for upper-extremity golf injuries [r8].
Modify forceful, repetitive and awkward-posture work with lighter loads, two-handed lifts and neutral wrist postures [r7].
Keep forearm, grip, shoulder and trunk strength up all year (expert opinion; no trial-proven prevention programme was identified).
Smoking and obesity were each independently associated with medial epicondylitis; this does not prove that changing them prevents it [r3].
clinicalPearls: Always check the ulnar nerve. Coexisting neuropathy was present in 16 of 30 surgical elbows and moderate or severe neuropathy predicted poor results [r4].

Resisted pronation is the most useful provocative test in the one series that compared them (positive in 28 of 30 elbows), whereas resisted wrist flexion was positive in only 12 of 30, so do not rely on wrist flexion alone [r4].

Avoid injecting by reflex. The one randomised medial trial showed a 6-week benefit that was gone by 3 months and 1 year, and in lateral elbow tendinopathy injection led to worse long-term recovery [r5,r6].
Do not assume a golfer has a medial problem. In amateur golfers, lateral epicondylosis in the lead arm is the leading upper-extremity injury, so examine both sides [r8].
In throwers, separate tendinopathy at the epicondyle from UCL pain just distal to it, because the two need different management and can coexist [r1].
Be honest about the evidence: most loading advice is borrowed from the lateral elbow and other tendons [r13]. Track outcomes in each patient and adjust the dose to the response.

forces.label: Wrist flexors and pronators work through impact

captions.text: A golfer hits a large bucket of balls, swing after swing, with a tight grip.
Through the downswing the trail forearm pronates and the wrist flexes, loading the flexor group.
At impact the wrist flexors and pronators work hard against the club's momentum.
Tension passes into the common flexor tendon and its origin at the inner elbow.
Swing after swing, with little recovery, the load can exceed what the tendon can tolerate.
There is no single injury moment: pain builds up as the tendon changes.
Zooming into the right elbow from the inner side.
The common flexor–pronator tendon anchors the wrist flexors and pronator teres to the medial epicondyle.
When you grip and swing, the flexor group pulls hard on its origin at the inner elbow.
With rest, the tendon recovers and adapts to the load.
With repeated loading beyond its capacity, the tendon swells and starts to hurt.
Pain is felt at the medial epicondyle, over the flexor origin.
The collagen becomes disorganised and thick. It degenerates; it is not mainly inflamed, and it does not tear.
The ulnar nerve runs right behind the epicondyle, so always screen it for coexisting neuropathy.
Healthy tendon: tightly packed, aligned type I collagen with a few resident tenocytes.
Reactive: after a load spike, tenocytes activate and the matrix swells. This can reverse.
Disrepair: cells try to repair the tendon and the collagen becomes disorganised.
Degenerative: areas of cell death and disorganised matrix remain, with limited capacity to reverse.
Progressive loading builds capacity: pain settles as the tendon adapts, even if structure does not normalise.
